title: [Netflix] Trading a Cloud Identity for Your Own: Workload Attestation on Managed Compute
summary: By Dhruv PratapIntroductionOrganizations that have been around for a while usually run two identity systems side by side. One belongs to the cloud provider: IAM roles, instance profiles, execution roles. The other is your own, and it is the one your internal services actually check when they decide whether to answer a request.On infrastructure you build yourself, you can bootstrap your own identity however you like. On managed compute you cannot. The provider hands your process a cloud identity and nothing else.This post describes how we close that gap for Apache Spark workloads running on Amazon EMR. A workload that starts with only an AWS identity has to end up holding a first-class internal identity. Doing the exchange is straightforward. Making it trustworthy is the part that took the design work. Very little of what follows is specific to Spark or to EMR.Two identity systemsInternal service-to-service authentication at Netflix runs on a private PKI called Metatron. Every workload gets a short-lived X.509 certificate, and services authenticate each other with mutual TLS. A workload cannot simply ask for a certificate. It is issued only after the identity service has satisfied itself that the requester really is the workload it claims to be. That verification step is called attestation. In each environment we support (VMs, containers, functions) attestation rests on some environment-specific proof that the platform can check on its own.The second concept is the Data Project, which is our unit of ownership for data. A Data Project owns tables, has a set of authorized users, and has an identity of its own. Jobs run as the Data Project rather than as the person who launched them. That is what keeps table-level access control and audit consistent across scheduled and interactive use.So the problem is this. A Spark job on managed compute starts with an AWS execution role and no internal identity. Everything it needs from inside the company (reading an encrypted column, evaluating table ACLs, holding an interactive session open longer than a short-lived token lasts) requires the internal one.One identity, one roleThe design rests on a decision made outside the Spark stack entirely. Each Data Project identity maps 1:1 to a dedicated IAM role, and the service that owns Data Project metadata records that mapping.The mapping is what makes translation possible. It lets a statement in the provider’s vocabulary (“this process is running as role R”) become a statement in ours (“this process is workload W”). Without it there is nothing to translate into, and no amount of cryptography helps. The hard part of bridging two identity systems is rarely the protocol. It is committing to a mapping and then keeping it authoritative.One practical objection arrives immediately. A single AWS account cannot hold tens of thousands of IAM roles, and we expect data projects in the order of ten thousands. We handled this by sharding data project roles deterministically across a small pool of dedicated accounts, which scales well past the projected number of projects and has the useful side effect of keeping workload roles on the far side of an account boundary from the control planes that launch them.ComponentsFive components take part.The control plane is the only service allowed to launch Spark jobs. It resolves the Data Project’s IAM role, builds and signs a workload metadata payload, and submits the job with that role as the execution role. It holds a signing key issued to it for this purpose alone.The Data Project service is the authority for the identity-to-role mapping.The Identity service receives attestation requests, verifies them, and issues certificates.A Spark plugin provides the hook. Spark 3.0+ added a plugin interface with driver-side and executor-side components that are initialized while those processes are bootstrapping.AWS STS acts as a notary, which is not its usual job.Step one: the control plane makes a signed claimWhen a job is submitted, the control plane validates the caller, looks up the Data Project’s IAM role, and builds a small payload describing the workload it is about to launch. The payload names the application identity, the mapped role, and the environment, stack and detail that the resulting credentials should be scoped to. The control plane signs the payload and passes it and the signature through as ordinary job configuration.Two properties of this step matter. First, only one service can produce a valid signature, so the set of things that can assert “this workload is legitimate” is small and auditable. Second, the payload is a claim rather than an authority. On its own it proves nothing, because job configuration travels through infrastructure we do not fully control and anything that can read it can replay it.Step two: the workload proves it holds the cloud identityWhen the managed service launches the driver process, it does so under an OS user that has the execution role’s credentials available. The driver-side plugin initializes and uses those credentials to sign, but not send, a request to the provider’s identity endpoint (sts:GetCallerIdentity). The result is a short-lived pre-signed URL.That URL is a transferable proof of possession. Anyone can fetch it. Only the holder of the role’s credentials could have produced it. And the response comes from AWS rather than from the workload, stating which role signed the request. The workload cannot lie about the answer because the workload does not supply the answer.The pattern is not new. It is the same idea behind AWS IAM authentication in HashiCorp Vault and in AWS’s own function attestation flows. It generalizes well: any environment that gives a process cloud credentials and nothing else can still produce a verifiable statement about its own identity.The plugin sends one attestation request carrying both artifacts, the pre-signed URL and the signed metadata.Step three: corroborationThe identity service does four things.It fetches the pre-signed URL against AWS STS and reads back the role that signed it. This is the provider’s statement.It verifies the metadata signature against the key issued to the control plane. This is the platform’s statement.It corroborates the two. The role AWS reports must be the role the control plane said it dispatched, for the identity the metadata names.It issues certificates for that identity, scoped to the environment, stack and detail from the signed metadata.Step 3 is the point of the whole design. Neither statement is sufficient by itself, and they fail in complementary ways. The provider’s statement is unforgeable but under-specified: it gives you a role, and a role is not a workload. It says nothing about why this process exists or what it should be allowed to be. The platform’s statement is well-specified but unverifiable on its own, for the reasons above. Put together, the signature says the workload was legitimately dispatched and the pre-signed URL says this really is it. Neither party has to trust the workload’s own account of itself.There is a tension here that we settled deliberately, and other teams should expect to meet it. The provider’s answer identifies a role, not an application. Deriving an application name from a role name is fragile string matching, and the session identifiers the platform assigns are not under our control. We chose to take the application identity from the signed metadata and use the provider’s answer only for corroboration. That costs a network round trip and a stricter signing requirement, and it buys a much clearer trust story.The fan-out problemA Spark application is one driver and up to thousands of executors, created and destroyed throughout the life of a job. Attestation designed around one process per host does not survive that.There are two defensible answers.In the first, each executor attests independently. This is uniform, adds no new trust boundary, and grounds every process’s identity in the same provider-verified proof. The cost is amplification. One large job can produce thousands of STS calls and thousands of attestation requests in a burst, which looks a lot like an attack and creates a hard dependency on provider-side rate limits.In the second, executors inherit credentials from the driver. The driver attests once and distributes credentials to executors over Spark’s internal RPC, which we configure with authentication and AES-GCM encryption so that only processes in the same application can take part. Load on the identity service stays constant. The cost is a second trust boundary and a driver that is now a credential distribution point.Considering our scale at Netflix here we went with the second approach. The general lesson is that identity amplification is a capacity question, and it is better to answer it on purpose than to have it answered for you during an incident.LifecycleCertificates are short-lived by design, so bootstrapping is only half the work. On self-managed hosts a system service handles renewal. Inside managed compute there is no equivalent hook, so the driver JVM runs a timer that re-attests on a fixed interval, well ahead of expiry. Credential material is written to a temporary directory readable only by the process owner and removed when the process exits.Executors do not refresh. They are usually short-lived, and an executor that somehow outlives its credentials can exit and be replaced, which is cheaper than making every executor a renewal client.The rule worth carrying into any similar system is that attestation has to be a repeatable operation rather than a bootstrap step. Anything that can only happen once at process start will eventually be the reason a long-running job dies nine hours in.Why this generalizesIf you run your own identity system and are moving workloads onto managed compute, the specific services here matter less than the shape of the solution.Anchor on one exchangeable primitive. A single authoritative 1:1 mapping between your identity and a provider identity is what makes translation possible. The rest is plumbing.Require two independent claims and corroborate them. One from the provider, unforgeable and under-specified. One from your control plane, well-specified and replayable. Trust the intersection and never either alone.Keep the signer scarce. If exactly one service can make the platform’s claim, your trust story fits in a sentence.Hook the layer you still own. On managed compute you rarely control the host or its init system, but you almost always control the runtime: a plugin, an agent, an entrypoint. Attestation belongs there.Decide the amplification policy on purpose. Distributed engines multiply every per-process operation by their parallelism.Make attestation repeatable and credentials short-lived. Renewal is a requirement, not a follow-up.What makes the result trustworthy is that no single participant issues an identity by itself. Not the workload, not the control plane, not the provider. And the workload, which is the party in the weakest position to be trusted, is never asked to vouch for itself.AcknowledgementsThanks to Amer Hesson for the Data Project abstraction, Nick Siow for the Data Project IAM role sharding, and Doug Clark for Metatron attestation.Trading a Cloud Identity for Your Own: Workload Attestation on Managed Compute was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
summary: By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen MareddyStratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more.Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions.Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts, live events, sports, ads, or regional ingests like TF1 in France.To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below:functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1resources: numCpus: 8 memoryInMB: 18000 diskSizeInMB: 50000 networkInMbps: 1000Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners.In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong.The Challenge: Over-ProvisioningWhen engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution.Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons:High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task.Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1, AV2, and spatial audio). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released.Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts, sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats, and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise.Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste.Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform.To understand the scale of the challenge, we analyzed historical usage across Stratum’s workloads. The telemetry confirmed our hypothesis: over-provisioning was frequent, wasted compute was compounding, and the sustainable path forward required a fundamental re-evaluation of how resource configurations are managed.Meet the Stratum Resource TunerTo address the challenges listed above, we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) to automatically right-size Stratum containers. Our north star is to ensure that users never have to manually specify the resource configurations. We started with a handful of high-throughput workloads with relaxed latency requirements, which account for the majority (70%–80%) of resource usage.As a quick note on terminology, we use “right-sizing” and “tuning” interchangeably in this post. “Downsizing” means decreasing resource limits, while “upsizing” means increasing them. Since our goal is to optimize for cost, this post focuses on downsizing.Automatic right-sizing is not enabled by default. Function owners must manually opt in on a per resource type basis (e.g., CPU, memory, network, or disk). Once enrolled, SRT operates without a human in the loop across five steps:Figure 1: SRT Workflow High-LevelCollect resource usage metrics across all executions of that function.Generate a recommendation for each resource type (e.g., CPU or memory).Verify the recommendation through experiments.Apply or reject the recommendation based on the results of experiments.Monitor post-apply metrics, watching for anomalies after applying the recommendation.“Recommendation” is a key construct in SRT and serves as the primary unit of operation. As SRT executes its steps, it promotes the recommendation through several stages:Figure 2: Recommendation State MachineCREATED: A scheduled workflow generated the recommendation.EVALUATING: Recommendation verification is running, and SRT is analyzing the results.APPLIED: All experiments passed, and SRT automatically rolled out the recommended configuration.REJECTED: At least one experiment failed, leaving the function configuration untouched.MONITORED: SRT monitors the recommendation during a post-apply soak period to verify stability.The sections below examine each of these stages in detail. To illustrate the flow, we will follow the real-world lifecycle of the VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function — a high-throughput video encoding function whose over-provisioned memory and CPU footprints were successfully tuned.Note that all operational thresholds and safety limits discussed below are fully configurable per function to accommodate varying workload characteristics and risk tolerances.Metrics CollectionTo make these recommendations possible, we need a solid metrics collection mechanism. Every Stratum container reports its function execution metadata, infrastructure dimensions, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk, and network) at sub-minute resolution.These metrics flow through Keystone, Netflix’s real-time event streaming platform, and land in two separate datastores:Figure 3: Metrics CollectionExecution summaries store: Stores execution-level summary metrics indexed in Elasticsearch for fast point lookups, serving as our short-term datastore for querying and inspecting individual runs.High-resolution long-term store: Stores raw, high-resolution usage metrics in Iceberg tables. While slower to query, it serves as our long-term datastore, holding months of history for resource utilization trend analysis.One record is written per execution, which is represented as a span. Here is how these records look for a single span of our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function.In Elasticsearch, the record captures the high-level summary of the completed span, identified by tags.stratum.spanId:{ "tags.stratum.spanId": "38536313f65f060a", "tags.functionName": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "tags.stratum.phase": "run", "tags.stratum.success": true, "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false, "tags.stratum.function.execDurationSecs": 26, "tags.cpuCount": 8, "tags.memoryInMB": 18000, "tags.diskInMB": 50000, "tags.networkInMbps": 1000, "tags.titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107", "tags.instanceType": "r7a.24xlarge", "tags.nf.region": "us-east-1", "ts": 1780743028000}In Iceberg, the record contains the same metadata, but adds the sub-minute resource utilization timeseries tracked during that span:{ "span_id": "38536313f65f060a", "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "phase": "run", "success": true, "start_epoch_secs": 1780743002, "end_epoch_secs": 1780743028, "runtime_secs": 26, "cpu_requested": 8, "memory_mb_requested": 18000, "disk_mb_requested": 50000, "network_mbps_requested": 1000, "titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107", "instance_type": "r7a.24xlarge", "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false, "env": "prod", "resource_usage": }Recommendation GenerationA scheduled Conductor workflow runs daily, reading the past month of usage data from Iceberg and generating recommendations for every function and resource type. The workflow also generates recommendations for functions that have not opted into automatic right-sizing to preview potential savings.Each recommendation is saved in the recommendations datastore, enabling us to query and filter recommendations by function, resource type, or status on an ad hoc basis.Figure 4: Recommendation Generation SequenceFor each function and resource type, the workflow applies the following generation logic:Filter by workload type: We only tune high-throughput workloads. This focuses our efforts on right-sizing, which yields the most meaningful fleet-wide savings.Aggressively tune CPU and network: We target p99 usage with no extra headroom. CPU and network are compressible resources; if a container occasionally hits these limits, the function might execute slightly slower.Conservatively tune memory and disk: We target p99.9 usage and include a safety buffer. Running out of physical memory or disk space causes hard failures — such as Out of Memory (OOM) or Out of Disk (OOD) crashes — making a protective margin essential.Apply safeguards to changes: We discard recommendations if the absolute reduction is too small to justify operational effort. For memory and disk, we clamp the maximum reduction allowed in a single cycle to 15% — a safety limit introduced after learning from early production runs.The workflow creates new recommendations in the CREATED state. If a recommendation already exists in this state for a given function and resource type, SRT overwrites it with updated calculations. Once a recommendation advances past the CREATED state, its recommended_value and stats fields become immutable. Subsequent daily runs generate a new recommendation with a unique ID instead of modifying the existing record.Here is how these recommendations look across resource types in their initial CREATED state for our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function:CPU recommendation{ "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "env": "prod", "resource_type": "CPU", "current_value": 8, "recommended_value": 4, "status": "CREATED", "resource_cost_usd_per_hour": ***, "stats": { "usage": { "p99": 4.16, "p999": 4.57 }, "execution": { "total_fn_executions": 748762182, "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75, "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723 }, "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" } }, "experiment_inputs": null, "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null, "outcome_message": null, "finalized_at": null}Memory recommendation (15% reduction in one step){ "id": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7", "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1", "env": "prod", "resource_type": "MEMORY_MB", "current_value": 18000, "recommended_value": 15300, "status": "CREATED", "resource_cost_usd_per_hour": ***, "stats": { "usage": { "avg": 5296.43, "p99": 6750.8, "p999": 7820.3 }, "execution": { "total_fn_executions": 748762182, "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75, "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723 }, "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" } }, "experiment_inputs": null, "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null, "outcome_message": null, "finalized_at": null}As the recommendation moves through its lifecycle, SRT populates the remaining parameters.When proceeding to the verification stage, SRT transitions the recommendation status to EVALUATING, records the target experiment settings, and links the active workflow execution tracking the experiment.Finally, once verification runs complete, the status changes to APPLIED or REJECTED, storing the outcome details and completion timestamp for analysis.Retry with More ResourcesWe take a conservative approach to generating recommendations, prioritizing system stability over extreme efficiency. Because recommendations rely on historical usage data, they cannot always anticipate sudden spikes or novel workload profiles when functions encounter heavy, unseen requests.To handle these unexpected spikes, we developed a fail-safe mechanism. A watcher process running in each tuned container tracks memory and disk usage during function execution. If the container exceeds the pre-set thresholds, 85% for non-cached memory usage or 95% for disk usage, the watcher flags the execution as high risk, cancels execution, and re-queues the task onto a larger container:new_container_size = original_container_size * 1.5This 1.5 multiplier only applies to memory and disk dimensions.Figure 5: Retry with More ResourcesThis “retry with more resources” mechanism serves as our safety net: larger container configurations are applied only when retrying tasks to self-heal from edge cases. Although these infrequent retries incur additional compute costs and latency, they allow us to keep day-to-day configurations highly optimized without having to size for rare, costly outliers up front.For our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function, if a heavy run causes memory usage to exceed the 85% threshold (15,300 MB) within its current 18,000 MB container, the system aborts the execution and reruns it on a 27,000 MB container.While we prefer to trigger retries based on actual OOM or OOD events rather than pre-set thresholds, technical constraints in our current architecture make true event detection challenging. Using pre-set thresholds serves as a reliable stopgap while we develop improved detection capabilities.SRT automatically enables the retry mechanism for any function opted into memory or disk right-sizing. Each Stratum container reports retry events, which flow into Elasticsearch and Iceberg alongside standard performance telemetry.Recommendation VerificationEvery recommendation must pass a two-stage verification process managed by a Conductor workflow before rollout. During this EVALUATING stage, SRT executes two distinct experiment types:Synthetic experiment: A low-cost, low-risk test to catch obvious regressions before production rollout.Production experiment: A live evaluation that validates changes across diverse production workloads to increase confidence.A recommendation advances to production testing only after passing the synthetic experiment. When an opted-in function has multiple pending recommendations, SRT prioritizes and evaluates the candidates with the highest estimated savings first.Figure 6: Evaluating StageSynthetic experiment:Runs in a test environment isolated from production traffic.Sets up two clusters: one for the current and one for the recommended config.Replays identical request sets across both clusters simultaneously without splitting traffic, exposing both configurations to 100% of test requests.Typically runs for 1–2 hours.Runs to completion without early termination checks.Figure 7: Synthetic Experiment FlowProduction experiment:Runs in production on real user traffic, split three ways:◦ ~90% remains on the main cluster (current production config).◦ ~5% goes to a baseline cluster (current production config).◦ ~5% goes to an experimental cluster (recommendation config).Evaluates recommendations against a similarly sized baseline cluster rather than the main cluster to preserve comparable traffic profiles.Typically runs from one day to one week, depending on traffic volume.Fails fast: cancels the experiment early if regressions are detected.Figure 8: Production Experiment FlowThe Stratum platform executes other experiments alongside SRT experiments. To avoid over-splitting traffic, SRT experiments run at lower priority and yield resources to active, higher-priority experiments.Traffic arrives in irregular bursts separated by multi-day or multi-week lulls. The verification pipeline accommodates these variable arrival patterns rather than expecting steady traffic.Back to our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 memory recommendation (18,000 MB → 15,300 MB), verification is triggered with:{ "recommendationId": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7", "syntheticExperiment": { "numberOfExecutions": 3000 }, "productionExperiment": { "enabled": true, "maxContainers": 20, // max containers shift to baseline & experimental clusters "upGateTimeoutMinutes": 10080, // time to wait for traffic to start flowing "maxRunDurationMinutes": 1240, // max time to run the experiment once traffic starts "minSamples": 500 // min executions needed on both clusters before evaluating }}Both verification stages evaluate recommendations against two sequential checks, terminating immediately if either fails:Retries with more resources: Restricts memory and disk downsizes to a maximum 1% retry threshold over the experiment duration.Execution time: Compares median runtimes to prevent outlier distortion, permitting up to a 10–15% slowdown relative to baseline, depending on workload, and is configurable by function.If a recommendation passes both verification stages, SRT updates its status to APPLIED and rolls out the configuration to the main production cluster. If a check fails at any point, SRT marks the recommendation as REJECTED and preserves the existing configuration. SRT sends notifications for both outcomes.For VideoEncoder.encodeV1, both stages passed cleanly:{ "outcome": "APPLIED", "syntheticExperiment": { "result": "SUCCESS", "samples": { "baseline": 3000, "experimental": 3000 }, "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 59.0, "experimental": 59.0 }, "slownessIncreasePct": 0.0, "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 } }, "productionExperiment": { "result": "SUCCESS", "samples": { "baseline": 50361, "experimental": 49790 }, "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 196.0, "experimental": 198.0 }, "slownessIncreasePct": 1.0, "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 } }}The recommendation moved to the APPLIED state, permanently setting the memory allocation for VideoEncoder.encodeV1 to 15,300 MB. We observed similarly clean results for the CPU recommendation, which reduced CPU allocation from 8 cores to 4.Post-Apply MonitoringPassing verification experiments does not mark the end of the recommendation lifecycle. Updated function code, modified input parameters, or underlying changes in the compute environment (Titus/EC2) can alter production behavior over time. To ensure configuration safety and foster feature adoption, we instituted continuous post-apply monitoring for applied changes.We monitor metrics for 90 days across two rolling time windows: a 30-minute fast window and a 24-hour slow window. Each window maintains specific alert thresholds: a 3% retry rate over 30 minutes or a 2% rate over 24 hours triggers an automated notification.At steady state, workloads exhibit baseline retry rates around 0.1%, with rates up to 2%–3% falling within acceptable operational variances. Most applied recommendations remained stable over the past three months.VideoEncoder.encodeV1 has operated on its tuned configuration for months without breaching thresholds. However, VideoEncoder.encodeV2 presented a challenging edge case: a 50% memory reduction passed all verification checks and ran stably for two weeks before an unexpected traffic shift drove retry rates above 60%.Figure 9: Unexpected Retries SpikeBecause early versions lacked automated rollback capabilities, engineers manually triaged exception cases. This incident highlighted the need for automated mitigation, prompting us to construct self-healing rollback functionality.Today, the two auto-revert windows look like this:Last 30 minutes: 3% retries warn us; 10% triggers an auto-revert.Last 24 hours: A 2% retry rate triggers both an alert and an automatic revert.Breaching an auto-revert threshold immediately restores the function configuration to its pre-recommendation baseline.Figure 10: Recommendation Auto-RevertWe intentionally maintain straightforward revert logic — restoring the last known stable configuration rather than attempting dynamic resource adjustments during an incident.The VideoEncoder.encodeV2 incident also reshaped our recommendation generation rules for memory and disk allocations. Rather than applying full target reductions immediately, SRT now applies smaller, incremental 15% step changes, advancing only after confirming stability at each step. Additionally, we introduced a global kill switch to disable automated right-sizing across all functions in case of unexpected issues or side effects.Additionally, we enforce a mandatory cooldown period — typically one week — before initiating new experiments on a function. Pausing adjustments allows us to observe performance across diverse production traffic patterns, identifying potential risks before applying subsequent recommendations.Where Are We TodayOversized containers and config drift don’t have to be an accepted tax of running serverless workloads at scale. By building the Stratum Resource Tuner, we transformed manual, risk-averse resource sizing into an automated, self-healing pipeline. Through real-world workloads and hard lessons from unexpected spikes, we’ve proven that continuous right-sizing can safely deliver significant gains in infrastructure efficiency.We initially focused on right-sizing high-throughput video encoding workloads, aiming for an initial 5% reduction in overall Stratum compute costs. For instance, VideoEncoder.encodeV1 achieved a 50% reduction in CPU usage and 40% in memory usage without compromising performance or retry rates.However, edge cases like VideoEncoder.encodeV2 highlighted key lessons: large single-step reductions can introduce hidden risks, and manual incident response slows recovery. These insights led us to enforce stricter safety guardrails in the Stratum Resource Tuner, including capping memory and disk reductions at 15% per cycle and adding automated rollbacks when retry thresholds are breached. Guided by these safeguards, re-tuning VideoEncoder.encodeV2 yielded a stable 20% memory reduction with zero subsequent incidents.Looking ahead, our key priorities include:Expand SRT beyond high-throughput encoding workloads to support a wider variety of functions and workload types.Further tune the resources in regions with constrained resource availability.Move from reactive alerts to proactive, automated upsizing for under-provisioned functions.Experiment with intentional upsizing for latency-sensitive workloads to evaluate performance gains and reduce function execution time.Upgrade our failure signals for OOM/OOD events from lagging indicators to leading indicators to improve tuning precision.If solving problems like this sounds exciting, we are hiring in our Warsaw office. Check out open roles here.CreditsSpecial thanks to Olof Johansson, Jakub Karczewski, Adam Mazur, Ethan Mathieu, Rosanna Lee, Ameya Vasani, Jean Barkhuysen, Paul Hieromnimon, and Adithya Prakash.

title: [Netflix] The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale
summary: By Emma Yanyang Kong, JJ Tan, Ishan Gupta, Lars Olds, Claire Campbell, David Fagnan, Ratna Kavuri, Rohan Gosain, Veli Balin, Minsu Jang, Louis GarciaIntroductionAny team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge, a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it.This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out.We believe:A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle.It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations.A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. In our work, an explanation is human-readable evidence for why a title was recommended based on what the member has previously watched, shown on the title’s detail page, which is the screen a member reaches by selecting a title from the homepage. We focus on similarity-based explanations, which connect a recommended title to one reference title the member has interacted with via shared attributes such as genre and tone. For example,A funny, heartfelt holiday romance about love and new beginnings, much like “My Secret Santa.”Quality matters here because a misleading or poorly grounded explanation erodes the very trust the explanation is meant to build.Everything that follows comes out of a series of controlled, user-facing online experiments we ran on the explanation feature, including a month-long experiment on the Netflix mobile app. In these tests we used an LLM to generate explanations, hundreds of thousands a week across a constantly changing catalog. Manually reviewing them at this scale isn’t feasible, so we deployed a second LLM to evaluate them.What counts as a good explanation is specific to our task. However, the way we build, align, and monitor the LLM judge for evaluating explanations should be reusable and generalizable across different tasks.The Lifecycle at a GlanceFigure 1 summarizes the four phases of our LLM-judge lifecycle and the data flow connecting them.Figure 1. The four-phase lifecycle of an LLM judge, and the data that flows between the phases.We start with Birth: Benchmark Data Creation, where human experts craft hard or near-boundary examples and human raters label them with pass/fail decisions and written rationales. We augment this with LLM-generated gray-area examples to build a richer benchmark dataset.Next, in the second phase of Training: LLM Judge Development, we tune the LLM judge to align with human labels and rationales from the Birth phase, using self-reflection to identify mismatches between the judge and humans, and updating the rubrics based on those mismatches and anchor examples. We iterate in this phase until our metrics show that the judge is sufficiently aligned with human raters.In the third phase, Deployment, we integrate the judge into the explanation generation system as both a gate and a critic. The LLM generator writes explanations, and the LLM judge scores them and either passes them through or blocks them and supplies a rationale that the generator can use for self-refinement and retries. Passed explanations are served to members, and low-quality explanations are gated.Finally, in the last phase, HITL Alignment & Drift Monitoring, we keep the judge aligned with humans over time. “Human-in-the-loop” here means a person is directly involved in the decision, not just reviewing outcomes after the fact. We benchmark the judge against trained raters, and a human approves every change before it is rolled out to the system. During each test we sampled a set of explanations each week (both passed and gated, with a bias toward newer items), had human raters review them with labels and rationales, and compared the judge against these human ratings. If drift exceeded a threshold, we triggered retraining and benchmark data augmentation. This closes the loop by feeding new human-labeled data and updated signals back into the benchmark and development phases.System componentsFour automated components appear across all phases, alongside the human roles that define, validate, and supervise them.Generator: produces the explanation text, optionally using prior judge rationales and traces as part of its prompt for revision.Judge: evaluates an explanation and returns a pass/fail label together with a written rationale. In the deployed pipeline, it acts as both a guardrail (gating bad outputs) and a critic (providing feedback for self-refinement).Reflector: revises the Judge’s rubric when the Judge makes mistakes. It updates the rubric based on mismatched examples, human rationales, and anchor examples. It tunes the rubric and does not directly evaluate explanations.Meta-Judge: checks whether the Judge failed an explanation for the right reason by comparing the Judge’s rationale against a human rater’s rationale.Human experts and raters: the experts who define the quality criteria; the raters whose labels and written rationales the Judge is tuned and measured against; the reviewers who monitor the Judge while it is running and explicitly approve any changes before they were rolled out.Phase I, Birth: Establishing Ground TruthEverything downstream depends on knowing what “good” means, so this is the most human-intensive phase. Our internal writing experts define the must-have criteria an explanation must satisfy, author detailed labeling guidelines, and hand-craft tricky adversarial examples. Those same guidelines do double duty. They’re both the rulebook for human raters and the seed rubric for the LLM judges we tune later.Why we built our own benchmarkOff-the-shelf LLM-judge benchmarks focus on general-purpose text evaluation and miss what makes our task specific. Explanations are short, item-specific, and context-dependent (each one is tied to a target title and one or two reference titles the member has watched). We also care about alignment to our own editorial bar, not just generic language quality. As a result, we built our own custom benchmark from three complementary sources:Expert-crafted adversarial cases: hand-authored pass/fail examples with known failure modes, the kind of edge cases nothing else reliably produces.Boundary examples: LLM-synthesized explanations that are deliberately pushed near the pass/fail boundary, then rated by humans. These capture the ambiguous cases that sampling from live traffic rarely surfaces on its own.Real sampled explanations: explanations sampled from the output of our LLM generator during test runs.Two details that matteredThe benchmark is not frozen. A monitoring pipeline (Phase IV) appends a fresh batch of human-rated explanations on a weekly cadence, so over the course of a test the benchmark tracked the current catalog and new usage patterns instead of going stale.Every “fail” label carries a free-text rationale explaining why the explanation failed. This looks like a small bookkeeping detail, but it is actually critical for the next phase, since those rationales are what we use to tune and audit the judge’s reasoning.Phase II, Training: Aligning the Judge to HumansThe failure mode: right answer, wrong reasonThere is a failure mode that does not show up in label-agreement metrics at all. A judge can agree with humans on the label, passing when they would pass and failing when they would fail, while reaching the right verdict for the wrong reason. On a dashboard it looks perfectly aligned. But as soon as you ask it to explain a rejection, which our pipeline does to steer self-revision, it can return misleading guidance.We therefore care about not just label agreement but also reasoning alignment. In our setup, the Judge is always asked to output:a label (e.g., PASS/FAIL), anda short natural-language rationale for that label.Here is an illustrative example. The member watched a musical, a family fantasy with a young heroine and a well-known ensemble cast. We recommend an adventure movie that is also a family fantasy with a young heroine, which is why the recommender paired them. But it shares neither the songs nor the ensemble cast.The label (FAIL) is correct, and the stated reason is reasonable at first glance. But it turns out to be incomplete in a way that simple label agreement cannot detect, as we show below.Reasoning-Aligned Rubric TuningWe tune each criterion’s LLM Judge with a procedure we call Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART). As introduced in the system components above, the Judge, Meta-Judge, and Reflector are distinct components. The Judge scores an explanation against a rubric and gives a rationale, the Meta-Judge compares that rationale against a human-written one, and the Reflector edits the rubric text itself. RART is how the three are combined into a training loop.Every Judge is a fixed prompt template parameterized by a rubric, so tuning it does not mean retraining the underlying model. Instead we iteratively refine the rubric text until the Judge’s behavior matches human labels and human rationales. At iteration i, the Judge is conditioned on the current rubric text and maps an explanation to a pair, a label and a rationale.R_i is the current rubric text, y_J(x) the label, and r_J(x) the rationale.At a high level, each RART iteration proceeds as follows.Score the training data with the current rubric.Evaluate weighted alignment metrics on a held-out validation set. If all per-criterion metrics exceed their thresholds, stop.Otherwise, construct an error-driven focus set of misaligned examples and hand it to the Reflector, which proposes a revised rubric.The key difference from a standard loop is how we define a “mistake.” Most self-improvement loops look only at label disagreements. RART adds a second class of error. The Meta-Judge examines the cases where the Judge and a human both said fail and compares the Judge’s stated reason against the human’s rationale. When the two diverge, that is a right answer, wrong reason error, and it is also fed to the Reflector. Concretely, the focus set handed to the Reflector is the union of two error classes:Label mismatches: examples where the Judge’s label differs from the human’s.Right label, wrong reason: examples where the Judge and the human both said FAIL, but the Meta-Judge finds their two rationales don’t match.So the Reflector revises the rubric from both ordinary label errors and right label, wrong reason errors. That second term is the core of RART. The Judge is pushed not only to match human decisions but to justify them in a way the Meta-Judge recognizes as aligned with human reasoning.Returning to the earlier example, the LLM Judge said FAIL and a human said FAIL, so a label-only check would register agreement. Placing the two reasons side by side shows what that check misses.RART routes it into the focus set, so the next rubric revision has to account for it.Since the Meta-Judge is an LLM too, we checked it against humans first. Trained human raters labeled a sample of agreed-fail rationale pairs, and the Meta-Judge matched their verdicts on nearly all of them.Alignment metricsWe run one Judge per criterion, each with its own rubric, tuned and scored on its own. So everything below is measured per criterion on held-out data. For each one we track three metrics.Specificity (fail-recall): how often the Judge correctly rejects bad explanations. This is the one we care about most, because a bad explanation that slips through the gate is a trust hazard.Recall (pass-recall): how often it correctly passes good explanations, which keeps coverage high and revision cost low.Reasoning agreement: on the explanations both reject, how often they reject for the same reason.Each criterion’s Judge gets its own three, and one can be healthy while another slips. That is also why the gate is strict. An explanation has to pass every must-have criterion to be eligible to serve.Ablation: does the reasoning signal help?To isolate the impact of the reasoning signal, we compare RART to an otherwise identical loop that uses only label disagreements. We call this baseline vanilla: same Reflector, same Judge, same data, but no Meta-Judge and no use of human rationales.Figure 2. Improvement over the starting rubric, per criterion, for reasoning-aware tuning (RART) and label-only tuning (vanilla).Figure 2 shows the result. On two of the three must-have criteria, vanilla and RART land in the same place, because the starting rubric was already near ceiling and the metrics had very little room to gain. On the third criterion, the vanilla (label-only) method degrades. The Reflector in the vanilla loop rewrites the rubric into degenerate forms, and specificity and reasoning agreement fall with every iteration, ending up worse than the rubric it started from. RART stays stable on that same criterion and lifts both, with a small recall gain as well. The reason is that a vanilla (label-only) optimizer can reach the right label through unsound reasoning, and unsound reasoning doesn’t generalize to new data. Anchoring the signal on the rationale prevents that. Reasoning alignment helps where there is headroom and doesn’t hurt where there isn’t.Phase III, Deployment: Putting the Judge to WorkOnce deployed, the judge sat inside the generation pipeline, gating and critiquing explanations as they were produced during our tests.Two roles for one judgeOnce we align the LLM Judge with humans, we reuse it in two distinct roles for every generated explanation:Role 1, the gate. The Judge scores each explanation against the must-have criteria and rejects anything that fails.Role 2, the critic. When an explanation fails, we don’t just throw it away. The Judge’s free-text reason gets appended to the Generator’s prompt, and the Generator tries again.The second role turns the pipeline into a generate → judge → revise loop, with the Judge’s critique steering each revision.Bounded retries, and why we drop rather than serveWe cap the retries. Each revision costs another round of generation and judging, and the gains flatten quickly. Figure 3 shows what the loop actually buys, on 1,000 generated explanations run through as many as 12 revisions with four generators. Every curve climbs, which is the Judge’s critique doing its job, but the steep part is early, and the gap between generators is obvious. Revision amplifies a capable generator rather than rescuing a weak one. In our test runs we used a budget of 3 retries with our strongest generator, and an explanation still failing after that was dropped rather than served.Figure 3. Cumulative share of explanations that clear the Judge as we allow more revisions, across four generator models.That “drop rather than serve” rule is deliberate. The two outcomes aren’t symmetric. A bad explanation is a trust hazard, while a missing explanation just forgoes an opportunity. When in doubt we’d rather show nothing, and most explanations cleared the bar within the retry budget.Do judge-approved explanations help members?Passing the Judge proves an explanation is good by our standards, but it doesn’t prove that judge-approved explanations are useful to members. To test that connection, we ran a one-time controlled experiment on the Netflix mobile app, explanations vs. no explanations on the title detail page, over roughly a month, with the pipeline generating and judging hundreds of thousands of explanations a week during the period.Members who saw explanations shifted their viewing toward titles they hadn’t watched before, and more of their browse sessions ended in a meaningful play. Both effects were statistically significant, and we saw no member-initiated takedowns or escalations about explanation quality during the test. The result worth carrying over isn’t the size of that effect. It’s that offline agreement with our raters was necessary for these explanations to work but never sufficient to show they help members. Only the online A/B test could establish that judge-aligned explanations are not just quality-compliant but genuinely useful.Phase IV, Monitoring: Keeping the Judge AlignedA judge that’s well aligned at launch won’t stay that way. The catalog shifts, and so does what counts as high quality. The lifecycle has to close the loop.The weekly human reviewFor each week a test was running, we pulled roughly 300 generated explanations for human review, stratified across the Judge’s decisions (served, revised, dropped) and weighted toward newer catalog items, where drift is most likely. The stratification stayed fixed week to week, so successive weeks were comparable. A panel of at least three raters reviewed each explanation, and the majority label was our ground truth. Those labels did two jobs. They told us whether judge-human agreement was slipping, and they grew the benchmark.Setting the bar with human disagreementThe panel also tells us how much the raters disagreed with each other, which turns out to be the right yardstick for the Judge. Rather than hold it to a fixed threshold, we score the Judge and each rater against the same majority label and ask that the Judge fall within the raters’ own spread.Take one criterion and one of its metrics, M. That week’s sample gives one value M(J) for the Judge and a set of per-rater values M(H) for the three or more raters on the panel. We requireso the Judge must score no worse than two standard deviations below the average rater. A harder week widens human disagreement and widens the band with it, so the Judge isn’t penalized for difficulty the humans also felt.Falling below the band on any metric-criterion pair is a drift event, which triggers re-tuning (back to Phase II) on the augmented benchmark. A re-tuned rubric never goes live automatically. Someone on the team reads the proposed changes and signs off before it reaches the running pipeline, and we keep the previous rubric for instant rollback.What human review catches that metrics can’tBeyond asking whether the Judge still agrees with human raters, the weekly review answers a second question. Are the current guidelines still asking for the right things?In the weekly review process, reviewers surfaced issues that did not show up in Judge–rater agreement. An explanation can use accurate attributes and still overstate how similar two titles really are. A single vague adjective (“exciting”, “fun”, “emotional”) can technically satisfy the rubric while saying almost nothing. Sometimes the reference itself is the problem, something the member wouldn’t think of as a comparable title at all, so the comparison lands oddly no matter how the attributes line up. Some genres show the same problem at scale. Stand-up specials can share similar metadata tags but differ completely in tone and cultural context, so a comparison may look justified on paper, not be bad enough for a rater to fail, and still land poorly with members. And some explanations meet every must-have criterion while still reading like generic “word soup” that does not help the user much.When recurring patterns kept appearing, we updated the Phase I guidelines, which seed both the raters’ instructions and the judges’ rubrics, so one revision updates both sides. Other times we added product rules outside the Judge, for example by blocking certain title types from being used as references.Drift detection catches a judge that has stopped agreeing with people. Only the continued human review tells us when our definition of a “good explanation” is too narrow or incomplete. We need both.Drift detection keeps the Judge aligned with the current rubric.Continuous human review keeps the rubric aligned with what actually works for members.What We LearnedFive lessons we think transfer to any team shipping an LLM judge:Invest in the benchmark before the judge. A modest, rationale-annotated benchmark beats a large label-only one. Those written rationales are exactly what make reasoning-aligned tuning possible. You can’t correct a judge’s reasoning if you never wrote down the human’s.Tune on reasoning, not just labels. A judge can reach the right verdict for the wrong reason, which looks fine on a dashboard but gives misleading feedback and doesn’t hold up on new data. In our ablation, the label-only loop degraded a rubric that the reasoning-aware loop kept stable.One aligned judge can serve many roles. Reusing the same judge as both gate and critic amortizes the alignment cost and keeps production behavior consistent across roles. Alignment is the expensive part, so get one judge right and use it more than once.Plan for monitoring from day one. A recommender platform’s items and members never stop changing, so an LLM judge, like any ML model, has to be watched and re-tuned if needed, not shipped and forgotten.Keep people in the loop by design, not by exception. Automating evaluation is not the same as delegating responsibility for it. In our lifecycle, humans set the standard (Phase I), supply the rationales the judge is aligned to (Phase II), decide the conservative default of dropping rather than serving a doubtful output (Phase III), and review a standing sample of live decisions and approve every rubric change before it ships (Phase IV). These checkpoints are much harder to retrofit once a judge is already making decisions on its own. The standing review also tells us what our rubric is missing, not just when our judge has slipped.Taken together, the judge extends the reach of our reviewers, and those reviewers are the basis for trusting the judge. That relationship is what makes it responsible to run this system at scale. An automated evaluator that no one audits provides no assurance about the decisions it is making.AcknowledgementsThis post summarizes our research paper, “The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge for Large-Scale Recommendation Explanations,” which has the full methodology, metrics, and ablations.Our thanks to the internal human writers and review experts who defined what a good explanation is and keep those guidelines current; to our Human Data Operations team and the raters they train and calibrate, whose labels and written rationales are what the judges are aligned to; and to the engineers across the team who built and operate the pipeline; and to our UI engineering partners, who built the member-facing surfaces that bring these explanations to the homepage.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Global Industrial AIoT Platforms
summary: We’re proud to share that Microsoft has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Global Industrial AIoT Platforms. We believe this recognition reflects our vision for the future of industrial operations: moving toward intelligent systems that continuously learn, adapt, and improve business outcomes. Read the full 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Global Industrial AIoT Platforms report As industrial organizations modernize, they need a foundation that connects operations across cloud and edge environments. Azure’s adaptive cloud approach, powered by Microsoft Azure IoT, Microsoft Azure Arc, Azure Local, Microsoft Fabric, and Microsoft Foundry, enables organizations to connect operational assets, contextualize data, apply AI-powered reasoning, and close the loop between insight and action. The shift towards learning operations The first wave of industrial digital transformation was driven by IoT, connecting operational assets and making industrial data accessible, at scale. That visibility remains the foundation, but on its own it is not enough. Industrial organizations are contending with skilled labor shortages, supply chain volatility, increasing customization demands, and growing operational complexity. Success now depends on turning operational knowledge into scalable intelligence that improves throughput, quality, resilience, safety, and sustainability. This is where Industrial AI and Physical AI create new value. Industrial AI applies intelligence to operational data, identifying patterns, predicting outcomes, diagnosing conditions, and recommending actions. Physical AI extends these capabilities into the real world, enabling autonomous or human-assisted action that learns from results and improves performance over time. Together with IoT, they establish a business learning loop: IoT helps organizations understand operations. The people learn. Industrial AI helps organizations reason over operational data, identifying patterns, predicting outcomes, and recommending actions. The systems learn. Physical AI helps organizations act, whether through autonomous operation or human-in-the-loop workflows. By measuring outcomes and feeding results back into future decisions, the process learns. The outcome is more than automation. It is a transition from connected operations to learning operations, where every cycle of understanding, reasoning, action, measurement, and learning improves the next outcome. As the loop compounds over time, productivity increases, resilience improves, expertise scales, and the business itself becomes smarter. Grounding the loop in organizational intelligence A learning loop must be grounded in the operational context unique to each organization. By applying AI through secure, governed platforms, organizations can capture and scale the knowledge embedded in their people, processes, assets, and operations, while maintaining control of the expertise and intellectual property that differentiate their business. As that knowledge becomes institutional intelligence, it can be applied across adaptive workflows that continuously improve from real-world outcomes, helping organizations turn operational data into a durable source of competitive advantage. To accelerate this journey, the recently announced Microsoft Frontier Company initiative brings together industry expertise and enterprise-grade AI engineering to help customers design, deploy, and scale AI systems grounded in their own organizational intelligence, so they can translate operational expertise into measurable business impact more rapidly. Recognized as a leader in industrial AIoT Gartner defines the global industrial AIoT platforms market as a series of seamlessly integrated technologies that deliver industrial data aggregation and curation, device management of industrial assets, ease of integration with IT systems, and the ability to unlock the value of industrial applications and AI. We continue to help industrial organizations transform by focusing on the areas our customers prioritize: Unified platform for industrial needs Microsoft’s industrial AIoT platform extends Azure from cloud to edge, providing a consistent foundation for managing and securing industrial environments while connecting data and AI across operations. Key capabilities include Microsoft Azure IoT Hub, Azure IoT Operations, Microsoft Fabric, and Microsoft Foundry. Together, these capabilities help organizations make data-driven decisions, boost operational efficiency, and scale AI across varied deployment environments. Comprehensive management and security Microsoft offers a unified management and security plane where millions of distributed devices and assets, from factory Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) to autonomous vehicles, can be managed as first-class Azure resources. Devices and assets connected through Azure IoT Hub and Azure IoT Operations are onboarded as Azure Resource Manager resources, enabling deep integration with Azure Device Registry and Azure’s control-plane AI capabilities for governance, insights, and automation. Microsoft is advancing a Zero Trust security roadmap across the device lifecycle, from trusted identity, certificate management, secure updates, and firmware risk monitoring to policy-driven deployments and integrated SecOps. Encryption, confidential computing, sovereign operations, and auditable patching help customers strengthen resilience and meet evolving regulatory requirements. Governed industrial data foundation Microsoft provides a unified data plane delivered through Azure IoT Hub, Azure IoT Operations, Azure Device Registry, and Microsoft Fabric. The platform ingests OT, IoT, and enterprise data; transforms raw telemetry into structured, semantically aligned signals; supports Unified Namespace and ontology patterns; and makes governed, reusable, AI-ready data available across many different analytics and agent systems. Support for open formats and industry standards enables interoperable digital threads, digital twins, and AI-powered OT/IT workflows, while low-code and no-code options let subject matter experts drive the creation of data pipelines and analytics. Agentic industrial operations Microsoft is advancing industrial intelligence through agentic operations. Agentic AI can operate in both cloud and edge environments. In the cloud, agents use ontologies such as Fabric IQ to understand operational context, monitor conditions, and collaborate with teams through tools like Microsoft Teams. At the edge, agents run within Arc-enabled adaptive cloud environments, using local semantic models to reason over site-specific data and assets, enabling intelligent operations even during periods of intermittent connectivity. For industrial teams, this can support practical decisions: detecting equipment anomalies, recommending maintenance windows, and prioritizing responses to quality issues or production constraints. Shaping the future of digital operations Ultimately, the future isn’t about connecting more things. It’s about creating intelligent systems that can perceive, learn, reason, and act, where every machine, every process, and every action makes the next outcome better than the last. By combining connected assets, governed industrial data, AI-powered insights, and intelligent action, organizations can create systems that continuously adapt and improve from real-world outcomes. We believe this is the future of digital operations: intelligent systems that learn and deliver lasting business value. Microsoft’s robust partner ecosystem can help bring local expertise and tailored solutions to every industry, unlocking new opportunities and delivering even greater impact. Whether co-innovating on industry-specific solutions or scaling AI adoption globally, our partners are essential to helping customers build confidently on Azure. title: [Microsoft Azure] Responsible infrastructure at hyperscale: Managing the full lifecycle of Azure hardware
summary: Every new generation of cloud infrastructure creates two jobs. We must deploy more capable systems quickly, and we must manage the hardware they replace responsibly. Even though these jobs happen behind the scenes, the results matter to Microsoft Azure customers. Newer systems deliver more compute capacity from the space and power available in a datacenter. At the same time, the reuse, refurbishment, and recycling of older equipment can extend the life of valuable components and return materials to the supply chain, ensuring cost efficiency and reliability. Managing this process starts early in the lifecycle, with the design of our silicon, servers, networks, and datacenters. It continues through years of operation. When equipment leaves active service, Microsoft Circular Centers help determine its next useful life. Discover more about Microsoft Circular Centers With new Circular Centers in Newport, Wales, and Sydney, Australia, this work now spans North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. These facilities help us recover components, prepare space for new infrastructure, and get more value from the hardware and materials already in our system. Getting more from every rack and every watt Cloud infrastructure must keep pace with the work customers want to run. That means increasing compute capacity while making better use of the space and power available in each datacenter. Compared with early general-purpose systems, today’s servers provide significantly more processor cores, more memory capacity, and network bandwidth. As shown in the chart below, Azure infrastructure has become both denser and more efficient over time. Since 2014, cores per rack have increased approximately 13-fold, while the power required to complete the same task has decreased by roughly 90%. For example, a workload such as code compilation that consumed approximately 100 watts on early systems can now be completed using less than 10 watts. This increase in compute density means we’re able to provide more server capacity to support customer workloads using the same datacenter footprint. By delivering more useful work from each rack, newer infrastructure helps improve resource efficiency while supporting continued growth and scale to meet cloud and AI demand. Source: Microsoft internal analysis using combined average data across general compute infra partners and Cobalt using industry benchmark performance such as SPEC CPU report and industry-standard utilization markdown. Azure Cobalt is one example of this systems approach. Our custom-designed cloud processor allows Microsoft to optimize silicon, servers, networking, storage, and software together. Cobalt 200 delivers up to 50% higher performance than Cobalt 100 and incorporates the latest Microsoft security, networking, and storage technologies. This constant cycle of innovation is one of the defining characteristics of cloud infrastructure. As new generations of cloud and AI infrastructure are deployed, older hardware is gradually taken out of service. What happens to the equipment being replaced? Giving hardware its next useful life Last year, Microsoft achieved a 92% reuse and recycling rate for decommissioned servers and components. However, at the scale we operate, retiring a server is a little more complex than simply sorting components into the correct recycling bin. Every server must be securely decommissioned, and data-bearing components wiped. Then we must decide how to recover the most value from it. Can the complete system serve another purpose? Can processors, memory, and other components keep working elsewhere? Which materials can return to the supply chain? Microsoft Circular Centers manage these decisions as part of our datacenter operations. At these facilities, our staff give decommissioned hardware a series of possible next lives. Complete systems can support Microsoft labs and training environments, help schools and universities teach technical skills, or be sold to qualified buyers for continued use. Components can become spare parts for other systems. Materials are recycled when reuse is no longer possible. Our Circular Centers operate as a connected global network. With recent launches in Wales and Australia, eight centers are now in operation across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. The network continues to grow, with a new center planned for San Antonio, Texas. We are also investing in technologies that improve the efficiency and scale of circular operations. Through automation initiatives with AI-powered capabilities, such as robotic disassembly and autonomous material handling, we are helping accelerate the recovery of components and materials. Making the most of every resource As demand for cloud and AI continues to grow, every part of the infrastructure lifecycle matters. We must get more compute from every rack and every watt, while getting more value from every server and component. Circular Centers help us do both. They make responsible recovery part of how we grow Azure, renew the foundational infrastructure, and build capacity for what customers need next. Learn More Explore Azure migration and modernization. Learn more about Microsoft’s silicon to systems approach to Azure Infrastructure. Learn how Microsoft Circular Centers are scaling cloud supply chain sustainability.
