title: [Engineering at Meta] Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI
summary: Last year, we introduced GEM, the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This spans dozens of surfaces and objectives, delivering seamless full-funnel optimization across awareness, consideration, and conversions. The 2026 generation of GEM shifts from isolated per-domain optimizations — such as Facebook, Instagram, Reels — to a single central foundation model. It learns from data and signals across all of Meta’s ads platforms, bends the scaling curve at LLM-scale computation, and delivers strong advertiser outcomes through post-training techniques that provide a larger latency budget without requiring real-time evaluation of all ad candidates — all on a substantially more efficient training stack. The result is simultaneous ad performance gains across every surface and funnel stage, and deeper understanding that better matches ads to what people are looking for. GEM has delivered 18.9% conversion improvement and 12% ad click-through rate (CTR) improvement across Meta’s ad surfaces and objectives, and additionally contributed 5.8%, 4.1%, and 1.6% conversion uplift on Facebook, Instagram, and off-site conversion for targeted users over the past year. These gains span both upper-funnel surfaces and deep-funnel optimization goals, driving stronger returns for advertisers. GEM advances the frontier of recommender systems in the following four areas: 1. Bending the Scaling Curve, Enabling 2.5x Model Complexity Challenge: Empirical scaling laws demonstrate that model performance predictably improves with compute, parameter, and data size using transformer model architecture. However, recommender system models do not exhibit similar scaling properties with transformer due to massive heterogeneous features and shifting distributions. Solution: We built an LLM-style architecture — Kunlun, co-designed with the latest GPU hardware, to make larger, deeper models substantially more cost-efficient and to enable long-context learning over user engagement history. We observed an LLM-like scaling law at our largest pre-training scale with 2.5x model complexity growth from earlier versions of GEM. The pattern mirrors frontier LLMs: more capacity and longer context produce emergent gains in ranking quality that translate directly into business results. 2. Efficient Intelligence Transfer From GEM to User-Facing Models Challenge: Serving a model at this scale in real time is prohibitively expensive and drives up latency, compromising both user experience and advertiser ROI. Solution: The structured representation, LoopFM, a state-of-the-art post-training technique, transfers GEM’s internal representations and sequential historical memory to downstream models. Through computation sharing, it doubles the intelligence transfer together with the knowledge distillation deployed in the previous version, at no additional compute cost or latency. We also introduced elastic pre-computation (Solaris) to harvest the gains from the upstream model. 3. Accelerating the Central Compute Engine With Large-Scale Cross-Surface, Cross-Domain Learning at Meta Ads Scale Challenge: Meta’s apps span dozens of surfaces — Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Stories, and more — with 3.6 billion people using at least one of our apps each day. Each surface and optimization objective previously had its own independent prediction system. As the platform grows in surfaces and objectives, so does the challenge of improving ad performance simultaneously. Solution: GEM accelerates one single, unified compute engine through the central foundation model that jointly predicts clicks and conversions across all surfaces, including Facebook and Instagram, and across every key advertiser objective from off-site conversions to mobile app installs. The generalizable representations learned on data-rich click tasks transfer into data-sparse conversion tasks. A new training recipe with cost-free data mixing and the domain expert framework makes this heterogeneous, large-scale learning tractable, with predictable scale and enhanced reliability. 4. Scaling Total Training FLOPs by 4x While Doubling E2E Training Efficiency Across Thousands of GPUs Challenge: Training a RecSys foundation model across thousands of GPUs at this scale requires careful orchestration of compute, parallelism, communication, and memory. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization while scale. Solution: We developed custom kernels with low precision and new 5D parallelism strategies co-designed with the latest GPU hardware and Meta’s training cluster, and optimized model architecture with infrastructure together to scale efficiently across thousands of GPUs. End-to-end training efficiency is doubled to 20-25% model FLOPS utilization (MFU) with 4x total training FLOPs, enabling GEM to train at LLM-scale at Meta (see full technical story in our companion blog on Training GEM at LLM Scale). Scaling Law: Bend Scaling Curve at Frontier Scale with Kunlun GEM introduces a new LLM-style model architecture — Kunlun. Compared to the previous version (Interformer), Kunlun delivers 2x performance gains with the same computation scaling. Kunlun is designed around the following innovations: Standardize and unify architecture framework by seamlessly interleaving lifelong sequence modeling with scalable recommendation-specific cross-interaction. Introduce scalable architecture through deep co-design with the latest generation of hardware, and computation reduction with almost no model quality regression. Innovate efficient sequence scaling to process longer user engagement contexts with offline sequence infrastructure. The scaling law pattern on the light-weight model of GEM with small parameter size. Efficient Architecture for Scaling Recommendations GEM’s Kunlun architecture effectively bends the recommender system scaling curve at frontier training scales by empowering ultra-long user sequences and massive user-item interaction features. For the following technical discussion, we define two types of features: non-sequence features (such as user demographics, ad content representations), and sequence features with a sequence of events, each composed of a set of features. This architecture introduces three fundamental advancements: 1. A Standardized and Unified Architecture Framework We advanced the LLM-style architecture to better capture the unique characteristics of recommender system models — specifically, heterogeneous features and data dynamics. Each layer consists of: Attention: customize the attention and feed-forward networks to capture the long dependency pattern in user behavior by adapting to data dynamics. Summarization Component: simplify and enhance the summarization architecture to extract critical user insights from sequences, effectively bridging sequence and non-sequence structure. Cross Interaction: expand to the mixture-of-experts (MoE) style design, enabling large-scale modeling of complex interactions between sequence and non-sequence features. 2. Introducing Scalable Architecture Through Deep Co-design We co-designed the architecture with the latest generation of hardware to allow it to grow deeper and wider efficiently: Computation Complexity Reduction via Block Attention: Replacing full self-attention with block-aligned sparse attention reduces the complexity associated with sequence length from quadratic to linear relative to window size, and uses only the window size that is a multiple of block size, friendly for the kernel without partial block size. Component Unification via Architecture Reformulation: Per-Example Feed-Forward Networks (pFFN) was introduced to adapt the traditional FFN to per-example distribution. We reformulated the pFFN component into attention operations through Generalized Dot-Product Attention (GDPA), speeding up training by targeting at unifying the model’s many attention-like operations into a single GPU kernel, delivering up to 2x forward speedup. Scalable Cross interaction through Expert Parallelism: Our cross-interaction component utilizes a scalable, MoE-like framework that employs model-expert parallelism, allowing each GPU to process a subset of expert sub-networks in parallel. 3. Innovating Efficient Sequence Scaling We introduced specialized component designs to make ultra-long sequences computationally tractable: Component Skip Connection (CompSkip): The computational skip mechanism selectively activates sequence modules in each layer, and only routes outputs through residual connections. By selectively deactivating the specific components, which is based on the assumption that the network can recover quickly after re-activating, we reduce FLOPS by 43% with negligible quality loss. Sequence Unification (OneSeq): We selectively unify user sequences chronologically after the event feature aggregation. This allows a single, unified sequence layer to process long sequences, even when individual events possess heterogeneous structures and features. In the system, we have different user sequence sources, some of which have different events features. For example, an event in a purchase sequence can be described by ad ID and account ID, while the event in a post sequence is described by actors and object ID. They cannot simply be unified from the data source level due to the different set of event features. It requires the flexible sequence unification approach to maximize GPU efficiency because of large-size tensor operations and minimizing operator fragmentation. The GEM Architecture. On the left is the building block, and right is an illustration of the computation skip mechanism. How Ultra-Long Sequences Matter The new architecture makes ultra-long sequences feasible. GEM scaled the long engagement context length by 2x in production, and further enabled the capability of scaling long context to 25x, demonstrating infrastructure capability at frontier scale. Along the way, we discovered: Prediction quality follows a power law with sequence length. The relationship is predictable and consistent across sequence lengths. Larger models benefit disproportionately from longer sequences. This creates a virtuous cycle: scaling compute makes the model bigger, which makes longer sequences more valuable. Scaling sequence length makes the model more accurate, which justifies more compute. The two scaling laws reinforce each other, offering investment directions to bend the overall scaling law curve beyond simply adding compute. Post-Training: Knowledge Transfer at Scale The value of the foundation model depends on how effectively its intelligence transfers to the hundreds of vertical models that serve ads in real time. GEM revolutionizes post training for recommendation systems through the structure representation with the deep historical memory from the central brain, achieving 2x of transfer effectiveness beyond knowledge distillation. Furthermore, async computation is introduced to a few domain-specific foundation models to transfer the knowledge to vertical models. Structure Representation at Scale Knowledge distillation is effective but limited in bandwidth: downstream models only receive a compressed view of GEM’s intelligence at each training process. To address the limitation, we introduce the precomputed structure representation, such as LoopFM, to understand and compress the central brain from the foundation model into a compact representation, and then structure it with deep historical memory. It enables the downstream models to learn the long context from our central brain. It consists of the following major components across the system: Understand and Compress Intelligence: We compress the intelligence from GEM into the compact representations, which are summarized from the important layers, and used to comprehensively describe the event (or data) that is processed by the foundation model. Structure with Deep Historical Memory: We structure its compact representation together with the representations that the foundation model previously generated for the same user into a sequential context window, capturing user intent dynamics across all surfaces and traffic through GEM’s memory. Learn from Long Context Intelligence: Downstream models will learn the structure representation with long historical context through the specialized architecture during both inference and training time. The representation generation process is precomputed and shared with the computation to generate soft labels of the foundation model for knowledge distillation without additional foundation model cost. The structure representation paradigm. Speculative Precomputation for Fresh Predictions Solaris keeps knowledge transfer fresher, precomputing the user-ad representation from GEM just before vertical model inference needs it. Evaluating the large-scale model inside a live ad request is not affordable, Solaris moves it in time: It speculatively precomputes foundation model embeddings for the user-ad pairs a future request is likely to need, and delivers them just-in-time on the serving hot path. Downstream models gain access to near-real-time foundation model intelligence without being constrained by the latency. Borrowing the idea of speculative decoding from LLM serving, Solaris works through the following major components across the system: Deliver Fresh Runtime Knowledge: It generates the user-ad embedding directly, giving vertical models real-time, point-to-point knowledge of how a specific user is likely to act on the exact ad candidate. Speculate Ahead of the Request: As multi-stage ranking narrows a live request down to its top ad candidates, Solaris evaluates those user-ad pairs with the foundation model in asynchronous background jobs. The computation carries no latency budget with elastic capacity while it can capture rich knowledge. Enrich Coverage Hierarchically: When an exact user-ad embedding is unavailable, the system degrades rather than drops. It substitutes an aggregate of the user’s own recent embeddings across the same ad groups, or borrows from behaviorally similar users. Solaris speculative precomputation. Large-Scale Cross-Domain Optimization: Optimize Across Surfaces and Funnels We further trained GEM with the ads data at Meta scale, including all-surface data (e.g., Facebook and Instagram Feed and Reels/video) and deep funnel optimization (e.g., off-site conversion, mobile app install). GEM powers the first optimized model that jointly predicts both CTR across all the surfaces and conversion rate (CVR) across the major optimization goals. Previously, each surface and each prediction objective had its own system. This means learnings from engagement patterns across platforms can more directly be used to understand its conversion behavior (e.g., purchase) across ad surfaces. This positions GEM as the central model and compute engine for ads recommendation across Meta’s advertising surfaces. Unlike LLMs with the static data, RecSys models need to deal with data dynamics and freshness as well as the diverse distribution across surfaces and traffic. To overcome the challenge, GEM built the first training recipe for the large-scale cross-surface, cross-domain unification through: A Cost-Free Data Mixing Strategy: It introduced virtual data loading from different combinations of data pipelines without physically merging data together and incurring additional storage cost. It can flexibly adapt to the current ads ecosystem where the downstream models still train with the specific surface or traffic data. We also design a data mixture mechanism to control the mixture proportions during offline and online training close to the real datastream order received in real time, mitigating instability for domain switch and overmemorization for the recent domain data. A Domain Expert Framework: A shared expert learns a unified representation across all domains, while domain-specific experts capture surface-specific patterns. Each domain expert benefits from both: the shared cross-domain knowledge and its own specialized knowledge. Experts are built on top of the Kunlun architecture framework. Training a RecSys Model at LLM-Scale Efficiently GEM now trains at LLM scale on several thousand of the latest-generation GPUs. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics and rich user & ads signal interaction patterns that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization for training a foundational recommendation model of GEM’s size. We measure training efficiency through E2E MFU, which decomposes into two factors: E2E MFU = Local MFU (compute efficiency) × Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency). Local MFU (compute efficiency) measures how well a single GPU’s compute units are utilized — how close the workload runs to the hardware roofline. Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency) measures how much single-GPU performance is retained when distributing across thousands of GPUs. This decomposition matters because it lets us treat compute efficiency and scaling efficiency as related but distinct optimization problems, each with its own dedicated set of techniques. Both must be addressed to maximize end-to-end MFU. We tackled these challenges through complementary compute efficiency and scaling efficiency innovations: Compute efficiency: Achieved through a customized recommendation kernel library — Jagged Flash Attention (JFA), GDPA, Block-Attention, etc. — and mixed ultra-low precision training (including MXFP8 attention and MLP) optimized for recommendation workloads, purpose-built to leverage the latest generation GPU architecture. Scaling efficiency: Topology-aware 5D parallelism with Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)-free collectives — 2D FSDP + Expert Parallelism for dense parameters, combined with Fully Sharded 2D Model Parallelism for sparse parameters — co-designed with Meta’s multi-tiered network hierarchy to reduce communication overhead. The result: We doubled GEM’s E2E training efficiency to 20-25% MFU over the past 12 months while scaling total training FLOPs by 4x. Training a foundation model at the intersection of LLMs and recommendation systems is a co-design problem, not a software problem or a hardware problem alone. This 2x efficiency gain came from carefully considering every layer of the stack for optimization — kernels, precision, parallelism, networking, and memory all had to move together. For the full technical story, see our companion blog: GEM Training: Train Meta’s LLM-Scale Ads Recommendation Model Efficiently. The Future of RecSys Foundation Models Looking forward, we are excited to extend GEM to learn from all of Meta’s platform data, capturing behavior across organic and ads engagements spanning text, images, and video. We’re building toward LLM-scale long context, giving the model the ability to reason over longer spans of engagement context. This will unlock better ad relevance and help advertisers connect with the right audiences more efficiently. We will continue to scale GEM on even larger compute clusters, opening new scaling opportunities. We are introducing AI-driven optimizations, such as ecosystem enhancement and architecture co-design, to accelerate future evolutions. These optimizations will iteratively refine model architecture in lockstep with hardware advancements, so that each new generation delivers more intelligence per dollar of compute. We will evolve the post-training paradigm with reasoning capability to transfer more of this intelligence to downstream models, further improving advertiser performance and user experience. title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: Prime Day 2026 by the numbers, Claude Haiku 5.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, and more (October 13, 2026)
summary: Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong. The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines All the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used. The number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Claude Haiku 5.5 is now available on AWS – You can now use the fastest model in the Claude 5.5 family on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS, at around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It’s the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence per task instead of fixing one setting for a whole workload. It pairs naturally with Claude Opus 5.5: Opus plans and makes the judgment calls, and because Haiku is fast and cheap, you can run many Haiku subagents in parallel for routing, classification, and small code changes across many files. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic for voice agents – You can now build real-time voice agents on a speech-to-speech Amazon Nova model with better reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, plus lower latency. That combination matters for multi-step work: a support agent can look up an order, check return eligibility, and start the return inside one conversation. It keeps expressive voices in seven languages, controllable turn-taking, and a 256K context window, and pairs with Strands Bidi Agents, now generally available, to get a production voice agent going in a few lines of code. Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection now detects data exfiltration and destruction – Amazon GuardDuty now looks past login anomalies to the queries themselves on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. RDS Protection for data activity builds behavioral baselines and uses ML-based anomaly detection plus threat intelligence to flag unusual data access, with no agents, extra infrastructure, or database configuration changes. This closes a real gap: once an attacker has valid credentials from phishing or a misconfiguration, their queries can look indistinguishable from your application’s. AWS Lambda supports OAuth for self-managed Apache Kafka event sources – You can now authenticate Lambda Kafka consumers through your enterprise identity provider, such as Amazon Cognito or Okta. Event source mappings previously supported only SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, and mTLS, which left teams in regulated industries unable to use Kafka ESM at all. Now you get the automatic scaling, batching, error handling, and event filtering of Kafka ESM with the same identity governance you apply everywhere else. It works with self-hosted clusters and managed offerings including Confluent Cloud, Aiven, and Redpanda. Amazon Redshift adds Apache Iceberg materialized views – You can now pre-compute expensive joins and aggregations once in Amazon Redshift and store the result as an Iceberg table in Amazon S3, registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. You create them with familiar SQL, and the results are immediately queryable by any Iceberg-compatible engine, including Amazon Athena, Apache Spark, Trino, and Snowflake. Redshift keeps them current by recomputing only what changed. There’s a good deep dive on the AWS Big Data blog if you want the details. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Introducing Strands Box: AI agent sandboxes powered by Dogwood – As more of us let agents run shell commands and call APIs without approving every step, isolation alone stops being enough. Strands Box is an open source sandbox (Apache 2.0, developer preview) that combines OS-level containment with fine-grained policies written in Dogwood, so permissions can depend on what the agent has already done. You can say “let the agent post to the incident channel, but no more than three times every 10 minutes” and have that enforced from outside the agent’s process. It also keeps real credentials out of the agent’s environment by attaching them at an egress gateway. AWS Continuum sets a new standard in autonomous code security – Related to that theme, AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing now integrates into your CI/CD pipeline in public preview, turning penetration testing into a deploy-time event instead of something that happens off to the side. Developers get findings with severity, affected endpoints, and remediation guidance right in the pipeline output, and the pipeline re-tests to verify fixes. How Postman runs Agent Mode for 40 million developers on Amazon Bedrock – A look at the architecture behind a feature serving a very large developer audience. Worth reading if you’re moving an agentic feature from a demo to something that has to hold up under real traffic. ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026 – If you lost track of a month that included a lot of model launches, this is a tidy catch-up in one place. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, and reserved seating is now open. The session catalog is live, so register and claim your spots in chalk talks, workshops, and builders’ sessions before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, and this is a busy stretch. Upcoming stops include San Francisco (October 13), Miami (October 14), Brisbane (October 16), Cape Town (October 16), Malta (October 16), and Mumbai (October 17). Here in Brazil, the community calendar has more editions coming before the end of the year. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents powered by OpenAI, Q3 service availability updates, Kiro workflows, and more (October 5, 2026)
summary: Last week, we announced a public preview of Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents powered by OpenAI, built on a customized version of OpenAI’s Agents API engineered to be AWS-native and integrated with AWS resources. You can now build agents optimized for OpenAI models that run entirely inside AWS with the identities, permissions, and governance controls you already use. You can choose an execution environment: self-hosted compute to use an existing development machine, container, or compute environment or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, for managed runtime sessions and configurable storage in your AWS account. To learn more, visit the Amazon Bedrock documentation. In addition, we are adding new frontier models on Amazon Bedrock to expand your model choices: OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol: An upgrade to GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol delivers exceptionally strong performance on agentic coding, computer use, and professional work. According to OpenAI, it approaches GPT-6 Astra across demanding evaluations at roughly one-fifth of the cost, giving developers more room to build and run capable agents at scale. To learn more, visit the GPT-6.1 Sol model card. OpenAI GPT-6 Astra UltraFast mode: Ultrafast is a premium speed tier for GPT-6 Astra, built for workloads where speed matters most. According to OpenAI, Ultrafast delivers up to 6x faster inference in the API, with up to 300 tokens per second. The Amazon Bedrock inference engine delivers the performance, security, and reliability required for production workloads. To learn more, visit the GPT-6 Astra model card. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5: Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a smarter, more efficient Sonnet and a step up from Sonnet 5, making it a natural upgrade for teams already building on Sonnet. It’s stronger for coding, completing well-scoped tasks as part of a larger coding strategy such as building and fixing features with Claude in the same session or verifying output against requirements. To learn more, visit the Claude Sonnet 5.5 model card. SpaceXAI Grok 4.7: Grok 4.7 builds on Grok 4.6 with better mixed-document handling, more dependable repo-scale coding with planning and error recovery, and enhanced browser-use agents for form fills and portal navigation. To learn more, visit the Grok 4.7 model card. Last week’s launches Here are some launches that got my attention: AWS Well-Architected Agent (preview): You can use an AI-powered agent service that analyzes your AWS environment to deliver targeted, contextual recommendations for improving your applications’ cost, security, performance, and resilience. The agent analyzes your infrastructure, understands your unique business goals, and delivers contextual recommendations. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL supports direct querying of Apache Iceberg and Parquet data: You can directly query operational data together with data stored in data lakes in Apache Iceberg and Parquet formats using your existing PostgreSQL applications and tools, without extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines or data duplication. Amazon S3 Tables support all Apache Iceberg V3 data types: Amazon S3 Tables add support for geometry, geography, unknown, and nanosecond timestamp data types, along with column default values, as defined in the Iceberg V3 specification. You can now store geospatial coordinates and nanosecond-precision event times natively instead of encoding them in strings or integers. For specific guidance, consult the relevant service documentation or contact AWS Support. Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and news items you may find interesting: Introducing Kiro workflows: Kiro workflows enable you to carry out complex tasks from start to finish with multiple agents and less supervision. We’ve been building Kiro itself with workflows, including the new cloud configuration, cloud sessions, and most of the workflow experience. Introducing Strands Decider: Strands Decider is one of a new class of decision models or system one models, a type of model that has been gaining significant attention since TypeSafe AI’s launch of Jev earlier this month. Strands Decider 2B is a small, open source, decision model optimized for fast experimentation, local development, and innovation. New FDE pathways for AWS Partners: On June 30, AWS announced the Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) organization, backed by a $1 billion investment, and extended this hands-on delivery approach to AWS Partners through the Partner-Led FDE motion. Now, AWS Partners have a structured way to build and validate that depth with three new Partner FDE pathways and credentials that recognize the applied proficiency required to deliver production agentic AI. title: [HashiCorp] Secure AI agents with HashiCorp Boundary
summary: Locally running cowork and coding AI agents are evolving from passive assistants into active participants in enterprise IT operations -analyzing logs, investigating incidents, assessing system health, and recommending next steps. While this can accelerate troubleshooting and reduce operational toil, enterprise adoption requires answering a critical question beyond improving productivity: How can an AI agent interact with infrastructure without creating new security, compliance, or governance risks? This blog explores how to leverage HashiCorp Boundary’s zero trust access model to provide AI agents with secure, governed access to infrastructure resources. To explore this challenge in practice, we used IBM technologies and services to create an AI agent that runs on developer workstation and is capable of investigating infrastructure incidents through natural-language requests. For example, a platform engineer can ask the agent to analyze a performance issue, gather diagnostic data from a target system, and summarize the findings. The key objective was not only to build an AI agent but to ensure that every infrastructure interaction remained secure, controlled, and auditable. The solution overview The AI agent enables a platform engineer to describe an operational goal in natural language: A sample prompt can be: “Investigate memory pressure on app-server-01 and summarize the findings.” The following diagram shows the architecture and workflow for an AI agent built with IBM Bob. The AI agent uses watsonx and Granite models to interpret an operational request, develop an investigation plan, execute the required diagnostic actions, analyze the results, and produce a concise summary for the platform engineer. When infrastructure access is required, the AI agent running on the platform engineer workstation initiates a login to Boundary, and the platform engineer completes the authentication on behalf of the agent. The AI agent then opens a Boundary-proxied session to the authorized Linux target to perform the investigation. Session activity is recorded, and audit logs capture authentication events, access decisions, grants, policy changes, and administrative actions. This creates a human-authorized workflow for an AI-assisted operation without relying on fully unattended infrastructure access. The zero trust layer As shown in the architecture diagram, Boundary provides the secure access layer between the AI agent and the target infrastructure. Rather than granting the agent direct access to systems, Boundary evaluates the authenticated user's identity, permissions, and target access policies before establishing a connection. This separation of access control from AI reasoning ensures that infrastructure access remains governed by enterprise security policies. Secure access with Boundary In this model, Boundary enables five essential controls: Identity-based authentication: Boundary delegates authentication to IBM Verify through an OIDC authentication method and applies access policies to the verified identity. Zero trust connectivity: The agent reaches the target only through an active Boundary session, without requiring the agent host to have a direct network route or VPN access to the target’s private network. Boundary workers proxy the connection to the target. Target grants: Least-privilege grants restrict network access to only the Linux targets required for the agent’s operational task. Secrets management: Vault stores or generates target credentials, including short-lived dynamic credentials. Boundary retrieves and injects the credentials when it establishes the session, without returning them to the agent or platform engineer. This ensures credentials are shared, leaked, stolen, or insecurely stored. Administrative control: Authorized administrators can cancel an active session, providing a kill switch for infrastructure access. Auditability and session recording Boundary captures the agent’s infrastructure activity within the same governed access layer used for human operators. Session recordings provide visibility into session interactions and the associated target, user, host, and connection metadata. Boundary also emits audit events for authenticated requests, session activity, and administrative operations. Together, session recording and audit events provide centralized evidence for incident reviews, security investigations, and compliance validation, helping organizations treat the AI agent as a controlled and auditable participant in enterprise operations. Demo The video demonstrates how an AI agent uses a Platform Engineer’s verified identity and permissions to access enterprise resources through Boundary with governance and auditability. Final thoughts As AI agents move from analysis to infrastructure action, enterprises must embed security, governance, and accountability directly into the workflow. Automation alone is not enough; organizations also need controls that govern identity, access, credentials, sessions, and evidence. In this example, we used watsonx.ai to support the agent’s reasoning, planning, and summarization; Boundary to authorize and proxy infrastructure access; Verify to authenticate the platform engineer; and Vault to manage and inject target credentials. Together, these technologies create a secure, governed model for agent-assisted enterprise operations. The agent can help perform infrastructure tasks while operating within the identity, access, session, and audit controls expected from human operators. Building the AI agent You can try testing this workflow out in your environment. There are several possible approaches, but you can build your AI agent and enable secure access to your resources using Boundary by setting up the services and accounts as described below: IBM Cloud and watsonx.ai: Create an IBM Cloud account and use watsonx.ai python SDK to build the agent. IBM watsonx.ai provides access to the foundation models and tools that an AI agent can use for reasoning, planning, and summarization. You can also use IBM Bob, an agentic development partner, to design and implement the AI agent through natural-language prompts. Alternatively, you can use the AI agentic frameworks of your choice to develop your AI agent. Linux host or cloud VM: Create a Linux host in your cloud environment or infrastructure for the agent to inspect. IBM Verify: Sign-up for an Identity Provider (IdP) like IBM Verify. Configure OpenID Connect (OIDC) and create a user account. A platform engineer will use this account to authenticate Boundary before the agent opens a session. You can also use other IdPs of your choice. HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP) account: Create a free HCP account, deploy Boundary and Vault clusters and complete the following configurations: Configure the Linux host as a Boundary target. Enable session recording for the target and configure an Amazon S3 or supported S3-compatible storage bucket and the applicable storage policies. Store the host credentials in a Boundary static credential store, or, preferably, configure a Vault credential library. Bind the credential source to the SSH target as an injected application credential. Credential injection removes the need for the agent to receive the target credential. Configure Verify as an OIDC authentication provider in Boundary and set the OIDC method as the primary method. Configure Boundary roles and grants to give the authenticated identity least-privilege access to the required target. Local development environment: Install Python and the Boundary CLI on your development machine. The AI agent developed calls watsonx.ai python APIs and connects to the target through a Boundary-proxied session after the platform engineer authenticates.
